## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why must the limit on what an agent's code can reach be enforced below the model rather than requested of it?_

Within a few turns, a coding agent can install a dependency, read its documentation, and run code that neither its operator nor the model wrote. Permission to invoke a command runner does not limit every file, process, or network service that code might reach. The runtime needs an execution environment whose enforced boundaries match the task: which resources are accessible, how much capacity may be consumed, which work persists between turns, and what must end before another task uses the environment. Those boundaries cost startup time and memory, so their lifecycle and provisioning policy are part of the design. Sandboxing bounds the authority exposure of H·S·A beneath running code while accounting for the state it retains and the horizon over which it holds resources.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Specify the resources and effects reachable by agent-run code under a stated threat model and task grant
- Explain why restricted names and shared-process execution do not contain arbitrary untrusted code or its resource consumption
- Apply scoped grants, attenuation, and credential brokering while distinguishing possession, permission, and enforcement
- Compare execution envelopes by shared resources, trusted components, workload compatibility, enforced limits, and measured cost
- Design task-local workspace continuity and controlled artifact export without inheriting another tenant's mutable state
- Constrain outbound communication and identify disclosure that remains possible through permitted channels
- Specify reset and provisioning policies with explicit workload, capacity, residual-state, and external-effect assumptions
- Calculate sandbox pool size, resident memory, and burst drain time from arrival rate, lease duration, and snapshot restore latency

:::

## The Agent Threat Model {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-threat-model}

Consider a threat variant of the connection-pool repair. The coding agent reads the README of a vendored dependency to learn how the library is configured. Near the bottom, inside an HTML comment omitted from the rendered page but present in the retrieved source, a line addressed to automated assistants asks them to upload the environment configuration to a diagnostics endpoint before running tests. The model then proposes a `run_shell` call that would read a cloud credentials file and post it to that endpoint. The command fits the tool's argument schema. A runtime that checks only whether `run_shell` is an allowed tool would admit it, despite the task granting neither access to the credential nor permission to disclose it.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_a.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the Authority axis highlighted in purple; Horizon and State axes unlit."}

*Authority bounded beneath the model, limiting what code can change, read, and send.*
:::

The typed action contract from @sec-vol3-tool-calling requires more than that tool-name check. A sufficiently specific adapter can reject the proposed operation before dispatch. A general-purpose command runner must also constrain what the code can actually reach after dispatch: it cannot rely on the command description to prevent a subprocess from opening another file or socket. Sandboxing carries the task's limits into the execution environment.

### Untrusted input and execution reach {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-cohabitation}

The README attempt is indirect prompt injection: attacker-controlled material encountered as task data attempts to redirect the agent's behavior [@greshake2023not]. @Sec-vol3-security-threat-model develops why a model cannot reliably separate such text from its instructions, and @sec-vol3-security-evaluation shows how the resulting attack success rate is measured; this chapter needs only the consequence that the rate is not zero. Message roles and provenance labels can distinguish instructions from observations in the interface, but they do not enforce filesystem or network access. The runtime must preserve its resource boundary even when the model follows the planted instruction. The same unsafe proposal can arise without an attacker, through a wrong path, an unintended command, or a mistaken choice of target.

Three conditions support this particular disclosure path: untrusted content steers the proposal, the executing code can read the credential, and a channel can deliver it to the endpoint. Blocking the read or the outbound request defeats that path. Keeping the credential outside the execution environment removes that particular secret from its reach. None of these statements means that the environment contains no other sensitive information or that every harmful action requires all three conditions. The source repository itself may be private, and a destructive local edit needs no network channel.

The design therefore starts by naming what is protected and what execution requires. For the repair, the runtime can provide a task-local source tree and writable test scratch while excluding the developer's home directory, unrelated repositories, and other tenants' files. CPU, memory, storage, and process limits prevent a runaway test from consuming the host's entire capacity. Any permitted download or artifact export needs its own communication scope. These limits belong to enforced configuration, not to a sentence asking the model to remain within the task.

::: {#dfn-blast-radius .callout-definition title="Blast radius"}

***Blast radius***\index{Blast radius!definition} is the set of resources and effects reachable by faulty or adversarial execution under a stated threat model and enforcement boundary, including what it can read, change, disclose, or consume.

1. **Significance**: It connects the task's intended scope to the filesystem, process, resource, and communication limits the runtime must enforce.
2. **Distinction**: A grant states what the task is permitted to do. Blast radius describes what running code could affect under the stated assumptions, including consequences of misuse within those permissions.
3. **Common pitfall**: Estimating reach from the tools the model is told to use rather than from the resources available to the code behind them.

:::

A threat model must also say which failures it considers. Ordinary application errors, hostile code inside the environment, and compromise of the mechanism enforcing isolation are different cases. A boundary that contains a faulty test program need not withstand a defect in its own trusted components. Choosing an envelope requires identifying those components and shared resources, not simply labeling execution “sandboxed.”

### Blast radius by authority level {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-blast-radius}

The authority levels of H·S·A describe what the task may do, not which sandbox implementation it must use. @Tbl-vol3-sandboxes-authority-radius applies those levels to the consequences the runtime must consider. The rows identify design obligations; the actual mechanisms depend on the workload and threat model.

| Authority level                                       | Exposure within the granted scope                                                            | Containment and control obligations                                                                                              |
|:------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$A_0$ (read access)**                               | Confidential information can leave through returned observations or another permitted output | Restrict readable resources and destinations; govern what information the return path discloses.                                 |
| **$A_1$ (sandboxed mutation)**                        | Candidate files and task-local artifacts can be damaged; execution also consumes resources   | Confine changes to the designated workspace, enforce resource limits, and prevent mutable state from passing to another tenant.  |
| **$A_2$ (retry-safe or compensable external action)** | Effects reach a system outside the disposable workspace                                      | Scope access to the external operation and enforce its retry or compensation contract; resetting the workspace does not undo it. |
| **$A_3$ (irreversible external action)**              | An external consequence may have no adequate reversal                                        | Enforce the required authorization or approval at the effect boundary, without a bypass through sandboxed code.                  |

: **Authority and execution exposure**: Task authority identifies consequences to govern, not a universal choice of isolation technology. Resource limits and mediated access remain necessary across the levels. {#tbl-vol3-sandboxes-authority-radius tbl-colwidths="[25,33,42]"}

Read access deserves emphasis because the README attempt needed no mutation of the credential file. Protecting a file from writes does not prevent its contents from leaving. At the other end, containing a command does not make its permitted external effect harmless. A payment or production change occurs outside the disposable workspace. Approval establishes permission under the applicable policy; it does not by itself establish that the chosen action meets the user's goal.

Containment beneath the model (principle \ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}) requires the execution boundary to be enforced outside the code being constrained. An isolation mechanism must be implemented by a layer below the code it controls [@saltzer2009], which is the same reason the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}) places mechanical bounds below the model. A model-side measure lowers the probability of a bad proposal, while only a check the proposal cannot modify bounds what it can do. In the README case, a filesystem policy can deny the credential read, and an egress policy can reject the diagnostics destination. These controls address different parts of the path. They need not fail independently, and some harm can occur through an allowed channel without either boundary being escaped. @Fig-vol3-threat-model traces the injected request and a permitted one through the same three enforcement points. The system should record what it actually blocked or observed rather than infer safety from the absence of an error report.

::: {#fig-vol3-threat-model fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where Each Boundary Acts**: Two requests steered by the same README text cross mediation, the execution envelope, and egress. The injected `run_shell` request is admitted because it is well typed, then stopped where it tries to read the credential. The dashed segment marks that the destination policy would also refuse its upload, a check on a different part of the path rather than an independent backup. The second request passes every check because each of its steps is permitted, so its disclosure reaches the approved service without any boundary being escaped." fig-alt="Five columns labeled model proposal, mediation, execution envelope, egress, and outside the runtime, crossed by two horizontal lanes. In the first lane, an injected run_shell request is admitted by tool admission, marked read denied by the filesystem policy, and marked upload denied by the destination policy after a dashed arrow; the diagnostics endpoint is marked not reached. In the second lane, a submit_report request carrying private source is admitted, allowed to read, and sent, and red arrows reach an approved service marked disclosure."}
![](images/svg/defense_in_depth_rings.svg)
:::

The boundary also has a lifetime. The repair's `src/pool.py` edits and test artifacts must survive between turns, but should not become the next tenant's starting state. Protected acceptance checks remain outside the agent's writable scope, while test execution can still require writable scratch. Ending the task must stop or account for its running work and reset the state covered by the execution contract. As Tool Calling established, a cancellation request is not proof that work ended, and even confirmed termination does not reverse an external effect.

The chapter develops these obligations in sequence. First, it examines why executing arbitrary code inside the supervisor's own interpreter does not supply the required boundary. Scoped capabilities and credential brokering then describe how authority reaches execution without unnecessarily exposing secrets. Envelope choice and task-local workspaces bound what code shares and preserves; egress governs its channels; reset and provisioning maintain those boundaries across successive tasks. The first engineering decision is therefore where the untrusted code runs relative to the software enforcing its limits.

## Why Restricted Globals Are Not an Execution Boundary {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-in-process-failure}

A data-analysis agent writes Python to summarize a CSV file. The runtime could execute that code inside its own interpreter, supplying only the data and a few helper functions. This avoids starting another interpreter and reuses loaded libraries. It also places the generated code beside the supervisor's state, connections, and credentials. Removing names from the script's globals does not separate those resources from the code that runs.

The distinction is between restricting an interface and enforcing an execution boundary. The tool checks from the preceding chapter can admit a request to analyze the CSV. They do not make arbitrary code inside that request safe to execute with the supervisor's reach.

### Names are not the reachable object graph

Suppose the runtime supplies a small Python helper named `total` and an empty builtins dictionary. The intended interface permits summing a list. In ordinary Python, however, a user-defined function also exposes a reference to the global namespace in which it was defined. The illustrative failure in @lst-vol3-sandbox-escape reaches that namespace through the allowed helper, without importing a module or calling `globals()`.

::: {#lst-vol3-sandbox-escape lst-cap="**Restricted names, reachable state**: A Python helper defined in the supervisor module retains access to that module's globals. Passing the helper into another globals dictionary does not relocate or isolate it. This is a failure example, not a sandbox implementation."}
```python
# Defined in the supervisor module:
def total(values):
    return sum(values)

# Intended interface for generated code:
restricted = {"__builtins__": {}, "total": total}

# An expression submitted to eval(expression, restricted):
expression = "total.__globals__"
# Its result is the helper's defining module namespace,
# not merely the restricted dictionary above.
```
:::

This example assumes an ordinary user-defined Python function and unrestricted attribute access in the evaluated expression. The returned namespace can contain references the supervisor did not intend to expose, including imported modules or application state. Which further operations become reachable depends on those objects and the process's permissions. The failure is already visible before any file is opened: the claimed interface boundary did not hold.

Rejecting this attribute would block this particular expression. That is different from establishing that all accepted programs are confined. A filter that removes selected names must also account for the objects it supplies and the operations available through them. The engineer needs a defined language and access policy, not a growing list of forbidden spellings.

The reason is a result, not a matter of diligence. By Rice's theorem [@rice1953classes], every nontrivial property of what a program in a Turing-complete language computes is undecidable, and "this program eventually reaches a process-launching object" is such a property. A name or syntax-tree filter therefore cannot be both complete and permissive enough for real analysis code. Attribute names can be assembled at run time, as in `getattr(obj, "__" + "globals" + "__")`, and the classes loaded in the process remain reachable by walking from any literal's type to the universal base class and enumerating its subclasses. Confinement has to come from what the code can reach, not from what its text says.

Restricted languages remain useful. A purpose-built expression evaluator can accept a limited set of operations over supplied values, and a validated bytecode runtime can enforce restrictions on memory and host calls. Those designs need their own implementation and resource guarantees. They should not be confused with evaluating arbitrary Python after deleting entries from a globals dictionary.

### Native libraries share the supervisor's failure domain

The analysis may call a native library to parse an image, manipulate an array, or execute a numerical kernel. If that library runs inside the supervisor process, its memory accesses occur in the same address space as the interpreter and control state. A memory-safety defect can corrupt that shared state or terminate the process. If a defect permits arbitrary native execution, the attacker can attempt operations under the process's existing credentials and controls.

This is a process-level failure, not automatic kernel compromise. A system call requests work from the kernel, which still applies its access checks and other restrictions. Crossing into kernel execution for that request is normal operating-system behavior. Compromising the kernel or another protected process requires a further failure or an already available right. Nevertheless, losing the supervisor's process can already expose its in-memory secrets, disrupt other tasks it manages, or destroy its ability to enforce the tool contract.

The practical question is which components must remain correct for confinement to hold. In-process evaluation can make the interpreter, exposed helper objects, native dependencies, and supervisor state part of the same failure domain. Restricting a script's names leaves those dependencies in place.

### Shared authority and shared resources

The code also inherits the execution context in which its operations run. Reachable open files, database clients, or network connections may convey authority that was never intended for the analysis task. Moving execution to another process separates address spaces, but does not necessarily narrow that authority: a worker running under the developer's identity may still open the developer's files, and inherited handles can preserve access even when names are hidden. The runtime must decide which identities, handles, files, and communication channels the worker receives.

Availability needs an enforced boundary as well. Code can consume CPU indefinitely or allocate excessive memory without reading a secret or opening a socket. Permitted file writes and process creation can exhaust storage or process capacity. A namespace filter supplies no budget for these operations. If execution shares the supervisor's process, terminating the offending process also terminates the supervisor; a timeout recorded by that supervisor is not, by itself, a way to stop the computation.

The design therefore needs accounting and controls appropriate to the workload: CPU and elapsed-time limits, memory bounds, and limits on process creation, storage, and output where those operations are available. The controller must remain able to observe and intervene when the worker stops cooperating. Enforcement may throttle, reject further work, or terminate execution, and the result must report what actually happened. As Tool Calling established, termination does not undo effects already issued.

For arbitrary tool code, the runtime should choose an execution boundary that protects its control state and enforces the task's resource and access limits. @Sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms compares the available envelopes and their assumptions; no single mechanism follows merely from the label “native code.” First, the design needs to state which authority may cross that boundary. A separate worker with the supervisor's full credentials is a separate process, but it is not yet a task-scoped grant.

## Capabilities and Credentials {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege}

Moving execution into another process separates its memory from the supervisor's, but does not necessarily narrow its authority. A subprocess running under the developer's account may still read that account's private files or use inherited connections. In the README attack, the task needs repository access, not the developer's credentials. The runtime must carry that distinction into the resources available to the executing code.

A privileged service that uses its own authority to fulfill an insufficiently scoped request can become a *confused deputy* [@hardy1988confused]. The problem is not that identity-based access control must be coarse: an access control list can express narrow permissions. The failure is allowing the request to exercise the service's broader authority instead of the authority delegated for this task. Capabilities provide one way to make that delegation explicit [@saltzer1975; @miller2006robust]. @Tbl-vol3-ambient-vs-capability contrasts the two ways of deciding what a process may touch.

| Dimension               | Ambient authority (identity and access control lists)         | Capability-based authority                                   |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Source of authority** | The identity the process runs as                              | Possession of an unforgeable reference                       |
| **Naming of resources** | Global names such as paths and network addresses              | Handles or tokens that designate the resource                |
| **Default reach**       | Everything the identity may touch                             | Nothing without a reference                                  |
| **Delegation**          | Typically the identity's rights, or a separately managed role | Any subset, down to one object and one operation             |
| **Confused deputy**     | Common when a request exercises the service's own authority   | Excluded when every access uses a designating reference      |
| **Revocation**          | A policy change for the identity                              | Expiry, a checked status on the reference, or handle closure |

: **Ambient and capability-based authority**: The two models differ in where authority comes from and how it is passed on, which decides whether a tool process can be steered into using authority the task never received. {#tbl-vol3-ambient-vs-capability tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

### Represent and enforce a scoped grant

A capability is an unforgeable authority reference designating resources and permitted operations. It may be a protected handle checked by a runtime or kernel, or a token verified by a service. It need not be a signed string visible to the model. The implementation must prevent the holder from fabricating broader rights or substituting another task's reference; a plain identifier with no protected binding does not provide that property.

Use $C=(R,O,P,E)$ as an abstract description of a grant: rights $R$, objects $O$, additional conditions $P$, and expiry $E$. This tuple describes authority, not a required token encoding. The conditions can associate different operations with different objects and bind use to a task or recipient. Listing read and write among the rights does not mean both apply to every listed object.

The tuple becomes operational as a check. A proposed access $a$ names an operation, a target, and its arguments. The enforcement point admits it at time $t$ only if every condition in @eq-vol3-capability-verdict holds:

$$
\text{admit}(a, C, t) \iff \text{authentic}(C) \land a.\text{op} \in R \land a.\text{target} \sqsubseteq O \land P(a) \land t < E
$$ {#eq-vol3-capability-verdict}

Here $\text{authentic}(C)$ means the reference is protected and bound to this holder, whether by a kernel handle table or by a message authentication code the issuer can verify, and $a.\text{target} \sqsubseteq O$ means the resolved target lies within the designated objects for that operation. A rejected access changes nothing and returns a structured observation the model can act on. The check is also cheap relative to what it guards. Verifying a handle or a message authentication code is a local computation, orders of magnitude shorter than the model call that produced the proposal, so mediating every access costs nothing a user would notice. The expensive part of capability enforcement is making sure no path bypasses the check.

For the repair, @tbl-vol3-scoped-repair-grant separates the resources an execution grant could cover. Paths are names relative to the task's designated workspace, not arbitrary host paths.

| Resource                                  | Permitted use                                                        | Excluded use                                                  |
|:------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Candidate source, including `src/pool.py` | Read and edit the permitted source files                             | Modify another task's checkout or the protected baseline      |
| Task-local scratch and test outputs       | Create, read, and update within storage limits                       | Consume unbounded storage or inherit another tenant's files   |
| Protected acceptance checks and fixtures  | Read permitted fixtures and invoke the designated checking interface | Replace the checks or alter their reported result             |
| Private repository service                | Request authorized fetches through the broker                        | Obtain the service credential or push to an unapproved target |

: **A scoped repair grant**: Different resources require different rights; authority over one row does not authorize the excluded use in another. {#tbl-vol3-scoped-repair-grant}

The grant also has a lifetime and enforced limits on execution and output. It permits the repair to make progress while separating writable candidate artifacts from the machinery used to assess them. Tests may need writable temporary files; protecting acceptance checks does not require making every test output read-only.

The binding between the grant and execution is the essential step. The runtime associates the admitted operation with its actual task, resolves the requested resource within that scope, and checks the required right and current conditions. Resource naming must resist indirection or concurrent changes that could redirect an allowed path to a different object. The version precondition from Tool Calling remains a separate check: authority to edit `src/pool.py` does not establish that its current version matches the proposal.

The executing code must then be unable to bypass the policy by opening another path, using an inherited handle, or contacting an unrestricted service directly. This can require restricted mounts, process identities, mediated interfaces, or other controls supplied by the envelope. The guest need not attach a capability token to every system call if the enforcement layer has already bound its accessible resources to the grant. What matters is the resulting reach, not whether a token appears in the request.

On Linux, the supervisor can act as a policy compiler. It verifies the grant, then translates the permitted paths and operations into kernel-enforced rules before it starts the worker. Landlock [@linux2024landlock], a Linux security module, lets an unprivileged process irreversibly restrict the filesystem hierarchies and network ports it and its descendants can access; a `seccomp-bpf` filter restricts which system calls the process may make and with which scalar arguments. The supervisor installs both, together with restricted mounts and an unprivileged identity, and then calls `execve` on the tool. The worker runs under limits the kernel enforces on every open and connect, without knowing the grant's format and without being able to remove the rules it inherited. Filtering on system-call numbers cannot inspect the contents of pointer arguments safely, which is why path restrictions belong to a mechanism that resolves paths inside the kernel rather than to the system-call filter.

Admission also cannot know every resource cost in advance. An input-size check can reject an oversized request before execution, but CPU time, memory, output, and storage consumption require accounting while work runs. The corresponding limits need defined responses, such as denying further allocation, throttling, or requesting termination. These are enforcement obligations, not predictions supplied by the grant's description.

### Attenuate delegated authority

Attenuation creates a grant that permits no more than its parent. Writing $\mathcal{A}(C)$ for the accesses allowed by a grant, the relation requires

$$
C_{\text{child}}\sqsubseteq C_{\text{parent}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathcal{A}(C_{\text{child}})\subseteq\mathcal{A}(C_{\text{parent}}).
$$

Narrower object scope, fewer rights, stronger conditions, and an earlier expiry can establish that relation. Consider the repair's edit grant, issued at time $T_0$, and two proposed children:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{\text{edit}} &= \big(R=\{\text{read}, \text{write}\},\ O=\texttt{repo/},\ E=T_0 + 300\,\text{s}\big) \\
C_{\text{test}} &= \big(R=\{\text{read}, \text{execute}\},\ O=\texttt{repo/},\ E=T_0 + 120\,\text{s}\big) && \text{rejected: execute} \notin R_{\text{edit}} \\
C_{\text{scan}} &= \big(R=\{\text{read}\},\ O=\texttt{repo/src/pool.py},\ E=T_0 + 120\,\text{s}\big) && \text{valid: } C_{\text{scan}} \sqsubseteq C_{\text{edit}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The test grant fails even though its lifetime is shorter, because it asks for a right the parent never held. Execution needs an appropriate parent grant or a separately authorized grant from the controller. A runtime that intends to support a test phase therefore includes execute in the grant it issues at the start, or issues a new grant for that phase, and then actively withdraws write authority when testing begins. Withdrawing write authority during testing is what keeps a candidate from modifying the fixtures and checks that grade it, the property sealed evaluation depends on (@sec-vol3-evaluation).

Attenuation can also happen without contacting the issuer. Chained-caveat tokens such as macaroons [@birgisson2014macaroons] let any holder append a restriction and pass on the narrower token. The issuer mints a root token with a message authentication code $\sigma_0$ computed under a secret key only it holds. A holder adds caveat $c_i$ (a path prefix, a rights subset, a turn limit, an earlier expiry) and replaces the code with

$$
\sigma_i = \text{HMAC}(\sigma_{i-1},\, c_i).
$$ {#eq-vol3-macaroon-chain}

The verifier recomputes the chain of @eq-vol3-macaroon-chain from its root key and admits a request only if every caveat is satisfied. A holder of the child cannot remove a caveat without the prior code $\sigma_{i-1}$, which the chain does not reveal, so a subagent or tool worker can narrow authority offline but cannot widen the token it received.

This relation constrains derived authority; it does not imply that every permission in a trajectory must shrink forever. A task can move from inspection to an authorized edit or test phase under an explicit policy. Nor does deriving a read-only child revoke a broader parent that the same holder retained. If a phase transition is intended to remove write authority, the runtime must withdraw or disable the earlier grant and deal with access already opened under it. Delegation must also preserve aggregate budgets: issuing several children must not silently multiply the parent's resource allowance. @Fig-vol3-capability-attenuation draws both constructions, the checked derivation with its retained parent and the caveat chain of @eq-vol3-macaroon-chain.

::: {#fig-vol3-capability-attenuation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind**: Panel A derives two children from the edit grant. The test grant is rejected because it requests execute, which the parent never held, even though its expiry is earlier. The scan grant is valid because every component is narrower. Deriving it does not remove the edit grant, so a worker that retains the parent can still write until the runtime withdraws it. Panel B shows the chained-caveat alternative, in which each holder narrows a token offline by folding a caveat into the next code, and only a verifier holding the issuer's key can check the whole chain." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel A, deriving a grant: a parent grant C_edit with rights read and write over repo/ has two derived children. C_test, requesting read and execute over repo/, is marked rejected because execute is not in the parent's rights. C_scan, with read over repo/src/pool.py, is marked valid. A strip below states that the worker keeps C_edit, so write stays usable until it is withdrawn. Panel B, appending a caveat: an issuer holding key k computes sigma 0, a holder appends caveat c1 for the prefix repo/src/ to compute sigma 1, a holder appends caveat c2 for read rights to compute sigma 2, and a verifier recomputes the chain from k and checks every caveat."}
![](images/svg/capability-attenuation.svg)
:::

The useful question is therefore not simply “is the child narrower?” It is “which grants and resource handles can this worker still exercise?” That question applies equally to a helper process inside one trajectory and to a delegated agent; coordination does not change the meaning of authority.

### End authority deliberately

An expiry states when a grant should cease to authorize use. It does not close an existing file descriptor, stop a running process, or cancel a request already accepted by another service. Revocation likewise needs an enforcement mechanism, such as a mediated reference whose current status is checked, combined with control over ongoing work where the policy requires it.

Suppose the repair's edit phase ends while a worker still holds a writable source handle. Rejecting new edit requests alone leaves that handle as a possible write path. The transition must stop or constrain the worker, revoke the usable reference where supported, or move subsequent work into an appropriately restricted execution context. The runtime must record what it has actually confirmed rather than equating a changed policy record with completed revocation.

External effects have their own boundary. A broker can stop accepting new requests after expiry, but a previously admitted remote operation may still complete. As established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency, a lease or cancellation request does not settle that effect or justify a retry. Environment teardown and readiness for reuse receive their full treatment in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset; here the requirement is that authority have an enforced lifetime rather than an advisory timestamp.

::: {#chk-08-confused-deputy-defense .callout-checkpoint title="Scope, attenuation, and lifetime"}

A repair worker holds read and write access to the candidate source. It derives a read-only grant for `src/pool.py`, retains the original grant, and opens a writable handle before the edit phase expires.

- [ ] Has the worker lost its write authority merely by deriving the child? Which references still matter?
- [ ] Could the child add test-execution permission while shortening its lifetime and still be an attenuation?
- [ ] What must the runtime address when the edit grant expires if the writable handle or a remote operation remains active?
- [ ] How can the test phase retain writable scratch while keeping the acceptance machinery outside the worker's writable scope?

:::

### Credential brokering {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-credential-brokering}

Scoped access still leaves a placement decision: must the executing code possess the credential used by an external service? Putting a repository token in the guest's environment or filesystem makes it available to code that can read those locations. A credential broker instead holds the selected secret outside the guest and uses it on behalf of an authorized request.

For example, the repair worker requests a fetch from its approved private repository through a host-owned source-service adapter. The broker checks the bound task identity, repository, operation, destination, and current grant, then performs the credentialed request without returning the credential. Permission to fetch does not permit a push or access to another repository. The worker can cause a narrowly authorized use of the credential without possessing the credential itself.

Brokering requires a supported mediation arrangement. An application adapter can make the upstream request directly; a proxy can attach credentials only where it can legitimately inspect and modify the relevant protocol exchange. A signing service likewise needs to authorize what it signs, not merely conceal its key. The egress section develops how the runtime constrains routes that might bypass these interfaces. If a tool genuinely requires a credential inside the guest, a narrowly scoped, short-lived credential reduces exposure but does not eliminate possession risk.

Keeping selected credentials outside the guest removes one valuable target from the README attack. It does not make an environment dump or repository content nonsensitive, and a brokered operation can still be misused within its permitted scope. Secret placement, access permission, and the appropriateness of an allowed request are distinct concerns. Security develops the latter problem; this chapter establishes where authority resides and how execution is confined to it.

Capabilities and brokering specify the resources the runtime intends to expose. They depend on enforcement that the running code cannot bypass or modify under the stated threat model. The next section compares execution envelopes by what they share with the host and which components must uphold that boundary.

## Choosing an Isolation Envelope {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms}

Capabilities and credential brokering specify what authority the runtime issues. The next question is what enforces that scope when the executing code does not cooperate. A short log parser, the connection-pool repair's compiler and tests, and a customer-uploaded binary need different execution interfaces. Choosing their envelope begins with those requirements and the resources that must remain protected, not with a preferred packaging format.

::: {#dfn-isolation-envelope .callout-definition title="Isolation envelope"}

An ***isolation envelope***\index{Isolation envelope!definition} is the enforced boundary around executing code, specified by the resources it exposes, the components it shares with the host or other workloads, and the mechanisms that restrict access and consumption.

1. **Significance**: It makes the permitted reach of an operation a property of its execution environment rather than a request to the model or program.
2. **Distinction**: A grant specifies permitted authority; the envelope helps enforce that grant against the code that runs. It does not establish that every permitted operation is appropriate.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating the name of a container, virtual machine, or language runtime as a complete isolation policy without specifying its configuration and exposed interfaces.

:::

The **trusted computing base** is the set of components whose correct operation the claimed protection depends on. Changing envelopes changes that set and the interfaces exposed to untrusted code. Fewer interfaces can simplify review, but counting system calls or source lines does not yield a numerical probability of escape. The useful comparison asks which failures the design contains, which components remain trusted, and which interfaces the workload requires. @Fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum previews the four envelopes developed below by the component a system call from untrusted code reaches first and the calls that finally reach the host kernel.

::: {#fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where a System Call Lands**: Amber boxes run untrusted code, purple boxes are trusted mediators, and the host kernel closes every column. A shared-kernel container sends every call to the host kernel through a filter. A user-space kernel traps and emulates each call and makes a reduced set of host calls. A microVM's guest kernel handles ordinary calls natively, and only device I/O exits to the monitor. Restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction and reaches the host only through imported functions. The columns differ in which interface untrusted code can reach, not in a ranked probability of escape." fig-alt="Four columns labeled shared-kernel container, user-space kernel, microVM, and restricted bytecode, each ending in a host kernel box. In the container column, an arrow labeled every call, filtered runs from the workload process straight to the host kernel. In the user-space kernel column, the workload process sends every call to a user-space kernel that emulates it and makes reduced host calls. In the microVM column, guest processes make native system calls to a guest kernel inside a dashed guest region, and a VM exit for device I/O reaches the monitor and hypervisor, which makes host calls. In the restricted bytecode column, a module in linear memory reaches a runtime with host imports only through imported functions."}
![](images/svg/isolation_spectrum_v2.svg)
:::

### Shared and interposed kernels {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-gvisor-vs-microvm}

A **shared-kernel container** confines host processes using configured operating-system controls. Namespaces restrict views of resources, access controls and system-call filters restrict operations, and resource controllers bound consumption. The host kernel still handles the permitted calls. A reachable vulnerability in that kernel can threaten the boundary, but an ordinary system call is not itself a compromise. Container isolation depends on both the kernel and the selected configuration; packaging code as an image does not establish either.

A **user-space kernel** interposes another implementation of the application's operating-system interface. For example, gVisor's Sentry reimplements application system calls in a memory-safe user-space process and obtains underlying services through a restricted set of host calls, while a separate file proxy, the Gofer, mediates filesystem access so the Sentry never holds host file descriptors directly [@google2019gvisor]. Applications depend on the interfaces that this implementation supports, so compatibility must be checked against the actual toolchain. This adds a mediation boundary rather than eliminating the host kernel or the need to constrain exposed resources.

### A separate guest kernel

A **microVM** places a guest kernel and its applications behind a hardware-virtualization boundary\index{Sandboxes!hardware virtualization} managed by a virtual machine monitor (VMM). Application system calls normally reach the guest kernel; host interaction goes through the configured virtualization and I/O interfaces. Gaining control of the guest kernel is therefore different from gaining control of the host. The protection still depends on the monitor, hypervisor, hardware, and exposed device and host-service interfaces. It is not immunity to implementation defects or misuse of permitted I/O.

The separation comes from the processor. With hardware virtualization extensions, the CPU runs the hypervisor in VMX root operation and the entire guest, kernel and applications alike, in VMX non-root operation. Ordinary instructions in non-root operation execute natively, including the guest's own system-call instruction, which enters the guest kernel without involving the host. Sensitive operations, such as writing control registers, reprogramming interrupt controllers, or touching a device register the hypervisor has not mapped, cause a VM exit, in which the processor saves the guest's state in a structure the hypervisor owns, the virtual machine control structure (VMCS), and transfers control to the hypervisor. Memory is translated in two stages. The guest's page tables map guest virtual addresses to guest physical addresses, and extended (or nested) page tables that only the hypervisor can modify map guest physical addresses to host physical memory:

$$
\text{guest virtual} \xrightarrow{\text{guest page tables}} \text{guest physical} \xrightarrow{\text{hypervisor page tables}} \text{host physical}
$$

A guest that gains full control of its kernel can rewrite the first mapping at will, but it cannot change the second, so it still cannot address a host frame the hypervisor did not map for it. That is the precise sense in which controlling the guest kernel differs from controlling the host.

Firecracker\index{Firecracker!microVM isolation} [@agache2020firecracker] is one example of a reduced-device VMM using Linux KVM. It omits the PCI bus, ACPI tables, and firmware, exposes only a few paravirtual devices (block, network, virtual socket, and a serial console) over memory-mapped I/O, and loads the guest kernel directly, which shrinks both the device code an attacker can reach and the time to start a guest. Its design also makes a useful boundary explicit: the VMM supplies virtual network devices, but host integration must enforce egress filtering. A virtual machine does not supply the task's network policy merely by existing [@firecracker2024design].

### Restricted bytecode and host imports {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-wasm}

A **bytecode sandbox** runs code compiled to an execution format whose runtime enforces restrictions on memory access and control flow. WebAssembly, for example, confines a module to linear-memory regions whose accesses the runtime bounds-checks or surrounds with unmapped guard pages, and the module has no system-call instruction at all; it reaches its embedding only through the functions the host imports into it [@haas2017bringing]. Those bounds do not make every object inside the module memory-safe, and an allowed host function can still perform a consequential operation. The WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) applies the capability model of @sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege directly. The host preopens specific directory handles at instantiation, every file open is resolved relative to one of those handles, and a path that escapes it, such as `../../etc/passwd`, fails with a not-capable error rather than reaching the host filesystem.

This option is useful when the workload can target the supported format and needs only a small set of host operations. A parser given an input buffer and an output interface need not receive filesystem or network access. Supplying a broad host import would expand its reach again. The runtime, compiler, and imported functions remain part of the protection's trusted implementation; execution time and memory growth still need limits.

### Where the system-call cost falls {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-syscall-tax}

The four envelopes differ not only in what they share but in where each request for an operating-system service is handled, and that decides both compatibility and cost. Every mediated call pays up to three terms:

$$
T_{\text{syscall}} = T_{\text{trap}} + T_{\text{filter}} + T_{\text{switch}}
$$ {#eq-vol3-syscall-tax}

$T_{\text{trap}}$ is the cost of crossing a privilege boundary, $T_{\text{filter}}$ the cost of checking or emulating the request, and $T_{\text{switch}}$ the cost of handing control to another thread or process to do so. @Tbl-vol3-isolation-transitions shows which terms each envelope pays and on which calls.

| Envelope                | Where a system call goes                                    | Terms paid, and on which calls                                                              | Host interface exposed                             |
|:------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| Shared-kernel container | Host kernel, after an in-kernel filter                      | Trap and filter on every call; no switch                                                    | The host kernel's system-call interface, filtered  |
| User-space kernel       | Intercepted and emulated by the user-space kernel           | Trap, emulation, and a switch or exit on every call                                         | A reduced set of host calls made by the emulator   |
| MicroVM                 | Guest kernel, natively in non-root operation                | A native trap for ordinary calls; a VM exit and a switch to the monitor only for device I/O | The monitor's devices and the hypervisor interface |
| Restricted bytecode     | No system-call instruction; host imports are function calls | A function call plus argument checks, only on imported operations                           | Only the functions the host imports                |

: **Where each envelope handles a system call**: The envelope determines which calls cross to the host, which cost terms of @eq-vol3-syscall-tax they pay, and which host interface untrusted code can reach. {#tbl-vol3-isolation-transitions tbl-colwidths="[18,27,33,22]"}

The contrast that matters for coding agents is between the middle two rows. Builds, package installs, version-control operations, and test runners issue many system calls for clocks, files, memory, and processes. A user-space kernel intercepts every one of them, while a microVM guest executes them inside its own kernel and exits to the host only when it touches a virtual device. System-call-heavy work therefore tends to favor a container or a microVM over a user-space kernel, and pure in-memory computation pays almost nothing in a bytecode sandbox. The magnitudes depend on the processor, kernel, and implementation, so the table predicts where to measure, not what the measurement will be.

### Match the boundary to the workload {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-envelope-choice}

@Tbl-vol3-isolation-taxonomy summarizes the decision. Start costs are orders of magnitude for typical configurations, not measurements of a particular product, and the last column is the default assignment produced by the rule that follows.

| Envelope                | Boundary and trusted components                                                 | Start cost (order)                            | Fits                                                                    |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Shared-kernel container | Configured host-kernel isolation; workload and host share that kernel           | Milliseconds to sub-second                    | Trusted or reviewed code; work with no secrets or shared state in reach |
| User-space kernel       | An interposed application-kernel implementation plus its restricted host access | Milliseconds to sub-second                    | Untrusted code with modest system-call volume and supported interfaces  |
| MicroVM                 | Guest kernel separated by the VMM/hypervisor and configured hardware boundary   | Milliseconds from a snapshot; sub-second cold | Untrusted native code, package installs, multi-turn coding              |
| Restricted bytecode     | Runtime-enforced execution semantics and explicitly provided host interfaces    | Microseconds to milliseconds                  | Pure computation, parsers, per-call tools                               |

: **Execution-envelope choices**: Each envelope trusts different components and pays a different start cost; the default fit follows from the code an action runs, the authority it holds, and how long it holds the envelope. {#tbl-vol3-isolation-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[17,35,18,30]"}

The choice follows from three properties of the action. The first is the code it runs. Pure computation over supplied inputs fits restricted bytecode, arbitrary Linux programs need a user-space kernel or a microVM, and a shared-kernel container fits code that is trusted or reviewed, or work with no secrets and no other tenant's state in reach. The second is the authority it holds. At $A_1$ the envelope is the whole guarantee, since nothing else stands between model-written code and the host, so untrusted native code receives its own guest kernel. At $A_2$ and $A_3$ the envelope must be paired with the broker and the approval gate, because no envelope can contain an effect that lands in an external system. The third is duration, the horizon exposure at work. A start cost that dwarfs a millisecond parser call becomes negligible across a trajectory that reuses its envelope for many turns, as Notebook \ref{nbk-08-envelope-amortization} shows.

Applied to the three workloads, the rule gives three answers. The parser runs in a fresh bytecode sandbox per call. The repair holds one microVM for its whole trajectory, or a user-space kernel if its toolchain's interfaces are supported and the measured cost is acceptable. The customer binary runs in a microVM that holds no credentials and has egress denied; if its requirements cannot be met within such a boundary, it is rejected or moved to a suitable execution service, not given broader host access merely to make it run. Each answer is a configuration, not a label, and holds only for the mounts, devices, routes, and limits actually applied.

Every option also needs resource governance. A program can exhaust CPU time, memory, process slots, storage, or output capacity without escaping. Limits must cover the resources charged to the workload, including applicable host-side helpers, not just what the guest reports. The supervisor must remain able to observe limits and intervene. A quota bounds a specified quantity; it does not eliminate contention on every shared cache, device, or service. Tests should include excessive allocation and runaway output alongside denied resource access, with the expected disposition recorded.

On Linux, cgroups v2 [@linux2024cgroupv2] supplies these controls for a whole process tree, whether that tree is a container's workload or a microVM's monitor and helper threads. `cpu.max` grants a quota of CPU time per period, and the kernel throttles the group for the rest of a period once the quota is spent. `pids.max` bounds process creation. Memory has graduated limits. Above `memory.high` the kernel throttles allocating threads and forces reclaim rather than killing anything, while reaching `memory.max` without successful reclaim invokes the out-of-memory killer inside the group. The graduation matters because a kill destroys the task's in-memory state without a chance to record it. Pressure stall information (PSI) [@linux2024psi] reports the share of time in which some or all of the group's threads were stalled waiting for memory, CPU, or I/O, and a supervisor can register a threshold and be woken when it is crossed. The supervisor can then compact, checkpoint, or deliberately terminate the task and report a resource failure, instead of learning about the problem from a process that has already disappeared.

Measure cost from admission to first useful work, as well as steady execution and teardown, under representative concurrency. A fast “ready” acknowledgment can omit deferred initialization. A syscall-heavy build and an in-memory parser need not rank two envelopes the same way. Startup can also be paid at different lifetimes, which is a separate decision from the mechanism itself.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-sandbox-envelope-amortization
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SETUP PER CALL VERSUS PER TRAJECTORY UNDER EQUAL USEFUL WORK
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Execution-envelope lifetime in this section.
# │ Goal: Isolate repeated setup cost without asserting a stronger boundary.
# │ Show: Equal useful work, setup totals, and serialized elapsed components.
# │ How: Charge setup N times or once, then add the same N useful calls.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class EnvelopeAmortization:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical timings, not measurements of a named platform.
    calls = 100
    setup = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner.sandbox_snapshot_restore_latency.to("ms")  # illustrative profile: readiness to useful work
    work_per_call = Q_(3, "ms")  # held equal under both lifetime policies

    # 2. EXECUTE: serialized setup and execution, without queueing or overlap.
    useful_work = calls * work_per_call
    per_call_setup = calls * setup
    per_call_total = per_call_setup + useful_work
    per_trajectory_total = setup + useful_work
    setup_saved = per_call_setup - setup

    # 3. GUARD: equal-work ledger and independently checked totals.
    check(useful_work == Q_(300, "ms"), "Same useful work in both designs")
    check(per_call_total == Q_(1800, "ms"), "Per-call setup plus useful work")
    check(per_trajectory_total == Q_(315, "ms"), "One setup plus useful work")
    check(setup_saved == per_call_total - per_trajectory_total, "Only setup differs")

    # 4. OUTPUT: unit-aware displays for all numerical inputs and results.
    calls_str = fmt_int(calls)
    setup_str = fmt_time(setup, unit="ms", precision=0)
    work_per_call_str = fmt_time(work_per_call, unit="ms", precision=0)
    useful_work_str = fmt_time(useful_work, unit="ms", precision=0)
    per_call_setup_str = fmt_time(per_call_setup, unit="ms", precision=0)
    per_call_total_str = fmt_time(per_call_total, unit="ms", precision=0)
    per_trajectory_total_str = fmt_time(per_trajectory_total, unit="ms", precision=0)
    setup_saved_str = fmt_time(setup_saved, unit="ms", precision=0)
```

::: {#nbk-08-envelope-amortization .callout-notebook title="Paying setup once or repeatedly"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical trajectory performs `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.calls_str` sequential parser calls, each requiring `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.work_per_call_str` of useful execution. Suppose preparing the selected envelope through readiness for useful work costs `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.setup_str`. Compare preparing a fresh envelope for every call with retaining one envelope for this trajectory. Hold useful execution time equal; no platform performance claim is implied.

**Math**: For $N$ calls, setup time $S$, and useful work $W$ per call, the included elapsed components are $N(S+W)$ for fresh-per-call execution and $S+NW$ for trajectory reuse. Both perform `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.useful_work_str` of useful work. Fresh-per-call execution adds `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.per_call_setup_str` of setup, totaling `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.per_call_total_str`. Trajectory reuse adds one `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.setup_str` setup, totaling `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.per_trajectory_total_str`. The difference is `{python} EnvelopeAmortization.setup_saved_str` of avoided setup.

**Decision**: This comparison isolates one cost, not total task latency. It excludes model calls, queueing, teardown, state transfer, and any performance changes caused by retaining state. Fresh envelopes require an explicit way to pass needed task data; reuse allows process state and modifications from earlier calls to influence later calls. Retaining an envelope for one task therefore needs a stated within-task trust and lifetime policy. It does not justify reassigning that state to another tenant or weakening access controls. Pooling and verified reset in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling address a different question: how to provide ready capacity without inheriting a previous lease's mutable state.

:::

### Device access extends the boundary {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-gpu}

If the repair or analysis needs an accelerator, choosing its CPU envelope is not the end of the decision. The design must identify which driver and device interfaces the workload can reach, how device memory and compute capacity are assigned, which failures can affect neighboring tenants, and how device state is reset before reassignment. A remote accelerator service can replace direct device access with a narrower request interface, but its service-side isolation and admission controls then become part of the system contract.

Direct device access also requires attention to direct memory access (DMA), through which a device reads or writes system memory. CPU address-space isolation alone does not describe that path. The Linux VFIO documentation [@linux2024vfio] explains why device assignment uses I/O memory-management protection and why the isolation unit depends on device and interconnect topology. Neither an advertised hardware partition nor exclusive allocation by itself specifies every driver, fault, capacity, and reset property. Verify those properties for the actual deployment instead of transferring a CPU-only guarantee to its accelerator.

The selected envelope now has a defined execution boundary, resource policy, and lifetime. The repair's files have their own continuity requirement: later tests need the candidate edits and permitted artifacts from earlier turns. That requirement can be implemented independently of whether a particular process or envelope remains alive. The next section develops the task-local workspace and the rules for retaining and exporting its contents.

## The Agent Workspace {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-cow}

The repair needs files to outlive individual tool calls. An edit produces candidate `r18`; a later command compiles it; another runs the targeted test and leaves a report. Starting a new process for each command need not lose those files if each process receives the same task workspace. Conversely, keeping a process alive does not specify which files it may change. The runtime needs a workspace policy separately from its choice of execution envelope.

That policy identifies the source baseline, the task's private modifications, permitted scratch space, and outputs eligible for retention. The developer's ordinary checkout should not become the working directory of arbitrary generated commands merely because it is convenient. For this repair, source edits and build artifacts belong to a designated task workspace. Protected acceptance checks and their trusted reporting machinery remain outside the agent's writable scope. Checks may still need writable scratch; protecting their implementation does not mean forbidding every write they perform.

### Share a base, keep modifications private

A full private copy is a simple way to provision a workspace, but repeatedly copying an unchanged repository and toolchain can be expensive. Copy-on-write separates the unchanged base from modifications made by each task. The runtime pins the base version and exposes a task-specific writable view. Reads can use unchanged base contents; a modification acquires private storage according to the implementation's copying rules. Another task should not inherit those modifications merely because it uses the same base.

A layered filesystem illustrates the mechanism. A read-only lower tree supplies the baseline, while a private upper tree supplies additions and replacements. The merged view presents the result to the program. Deleting a lower-layer name requires a marker that hides it, rather than deleting the shared original. Linux OverlayFS calls such a marker a *whiteout*. Its copy-up and directory operations also involve metadata, so the upper tree is not simply a ready-to-submit source patch. The kernel's OverlayFS documentation [@linux2024overlayfs] describes these distinctions.

Copy-on-write is a storage choice, not an additional permission grant or a complete isolation boundary. The envelope must still prevent access to another task's private storage and unauthorized writes to the base. A microVM may use a private disk snapshot rather than a host-mounted overlay. Which data and caches are actually shared depends on that arrangement; sharing an image does not establish that every guest shares one host page-cache copy.

### Price the first modification

Copy-on-write moves some copying from provisioning to mutation. Its granularity therefore matters. A file-level scheme may copy a whole large fixture before a small in-place change. A block-level scheme can preserve unchanged blocks while allocating private storage for affected blocks. Filesystem cloning can also share extents where supported. These alternatives change the work performed, but none universally makes cloning constant-time or a one-byte edit a one-byte device write.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-sandbox-workspace-cost
#| echo: false
# What: Compare full-copy and copy-on-write provisioning payloads, then
#       first-mutation payload copying under two granularity assumptions.
# How: Payload bytes per design; a lower bound on time at one drive's
#      sequential rate (registry); one-byte change in a shared fixture.
from mlsysim import *

class WorkspaceCost:
    # LOAD: Hypothetical workspace sizes, not a particular filesystem benchmark.
    disk_bw = Hardware.Tech.Storage.NvmeGen4.bandwidth  # one local drive, sequential
    trajectories = 32
    base_image = 2.4 * GB  # scenario: repository, toolchain, and dependencies
    written = 40 * MB  # scenario: edits and build outputs per workspace
    fixture = 1.2 * GB
    block = 64 * KiB
    modified_per_workspace = 1 * byte

    # EXECUTE: Provisioning payloads, then one full-file or one block copy.
    full_copy = trajectories * base_image
    overlay_written = trajectories * written
    full_copy_time = (full_copy / disk_bw).to("s")
    overlay_time = (overlay_written / disk_bw).to("s")
    copy_vs_overlay = (full_copy / overlay_written).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    file_copy = trajectories * fixture
    block_copy = trajectories * block
    logical_changes = trajectories * modified_per_workspace

    # GUARD: Separate requested mutations from payload-copy accounting.
    check(abs(file_copy.to(GB).magnitude - 38.4) < 1e-12, "File-copy total")
    check(block_copy.to(MiB).magnitude == 2, "One private block per workspace")
    check(logical_changes.to(byte).magnitude == 32, "Requested logical changes")
    check(block_copy < file_copy, "Copy granularity changes copied payload")
    check(abs(full_copy.to(GB).magnitude - 76.8) < 1e-9, "Full-copy provisioning total")
    check(abs(copy_vs_overlay - 60) < 1e-9, "Copy payload is base image over written bytes")

    # OUTPUT: Typed quantities and shared formatters for the notebook.
    trajectories_str = fmt_count(trajectories * count)
    disk_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(disk_bw, unit="GB/s", precision=0)
    base_image_str = fmt_memory(base_image, unit=GB, precision=1)
    written_str = fmt_memory(written, unit=MB, precision=0)
    full_copy_str = fmt_memory(full_copy, unit=GB, precision=1)
    overlay_written_str = fmt_memory(overlay_written, unit=GB, precision=2)
    full_copy_time_str = fmt_time(full_copy_time, unit="s", precision=1)
    overlay_time_str = fmt_time(overlay_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    copy_vs_overlay_mult_str = fmt_multiple(copy_vs_overlay, precision=0)
    fixture_str = fmt_memory(fixture, unit=GB, precision=1)
    block_str = fmt_memory(block, unit=KB, precision=3)
    modified_str = fmt_count(modified_per_workspace.to(byte).magnitude * count)
    file_copy_str = fmt_memory(file_copy, unit=GB, precision=1)
    block_copy_str = fmt_memory(block_copy, unit=MB, precision=2)
    logical_changes_str = fmt_memory(logical_changes, unit=byte, precision=0)
```

::: {#nbk-08-workspace-copy-vs-overlay .callout-notebook title="Provisioning by copy, and the granularity of a first modification"}

**Problem**: An evaluation host starts `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` workspaces for the same task. The pinned base (repository, toolchain, and dependencies) is `{python} WorkspaceCost.base_image_str`, and each task writes about `{python} WorkspaceCost.written_str` of edits and build outputs. The workspaces share one local drive with a sequential rate of `{python} WorkspaceCost.disk_bw_str`. How much payload does a full private copy move compared with a copy-on-write view, and what does a later one-byte change to a shared file cost?

**Provisioning**: A full copy moves `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` × `{python} WorkspaceCost.base_image_str` = `{python} WorkspaceCost.full_copy_str` before any agent runs, at least `{python} WorkspaceCost.full_copy_time_str` of drive time even at the sequential rate. A copy-on-write view starts as a mount, and only written data acquires private storage, `{python} WorkspaceCost.overlay_written_str` across all tasks, at least `{python} WorkspaceCost.overlay_time_str`. The copy moves `{python} WorkspaceCost.copy_vs_overlay_mult_str` as many bytes, and the ratio is simply the base size over the bytes each task writes. Copy-on-write makes provisioning cost track what the agent changes, not what it can see.

**First modification**: Each of `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` independent workspaces initially shares an unchanged `{python} WorkspaceCost.fixture_str` binary fixture. Each task overwrites `{python} WorkspaceCost.modified_str` byte within that fixture. Compare two hypothetical implementations: the first copies the entire file's payload into private storage before modifying it; the second copies only the one `{python} WorkspaceCost.block_str` block containing the update. Assume that block was shared before the update and that no other block needs copying. Neither implementation uses a copy offload or compression in this accounting.

**Calculation**: File-granularity copying moves `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` × `{python} WorkspaceCost.fixture_str` = `{python} WorkspaceCost.file_copy_str` of payload. Under the stipulated block-copy rule, the corresponding total is `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` × `{python} WorkspaceCost.block_str` $\approx$ `{python} WorkspaceCost.block_copy_str`. Both support the same `{python} WorkspaceCost.logical_changes_str` of requested logical changes.

**Systems insight**: The first-write cost follows the copying unit, not just the size of the edit. These totals count payload copied under the two assumptions, excluding metadata and the update itself; they are not physical device-write counts. Caching, allocation, journaling, and the storage implementation affect actual traffic and latency, so a sequential-rate division gives only a lower bound on time, never an estimate of it.

:::

The design response follows the workload. Keep large immutable fixtures read-only when tests do not need to modify them. Place new logs and build outputs in bounded scratch storage rather than repeatedly modifying large shared files. When tasks genuinely change large datasets, evaluate block-level snapshots or supported extent-sharing mechanisms against their access pattern. Copy-on-write can avoid copying untouched data, but offers less benefit when most of the base changes.

Private storage still needs limits. Bound allocated bytes and file counts, account for retained logs and caches, and govern I/O work alongside the execution limits already established. A quota failure must reach the tool result as a resource failure, not a successful but mysteriously incomplete artifact. Per-workspace quotas also need host-level admission and capacity accounting: many individually bounded workspaces can exhaust a shared pool.

### Own the workspace lifetime {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-lease}

A workspace lease binds the workspace to its task, owner, permitted operations, and lifetime. The runtime records which envelope, jobs, and access channels can use it. This permits the repair's edits and selected caches to remain available across turns without silently making them available to the next tenant. A new process can receive the same workspace under that lease; a new unrelated task requires its own authorized state.

The lease is an ownership and lifetime contract, not a duplicate-execution guarantee. Renewing or replacing it does not establish whether an earlier tool operation took effect. Nor does expiry prove that a running test stopped or an existing file handle became unusable. The runtime must enforce the end of access on the resources it controls, including already running work. The retry and pending-job distinctions from @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async still apply.

Before discarding private state, preserve only outputs the task permits to leave. For the repair, that may mean a patch relative to the pinned baseline, the resulting source version, and selected check records. Export from a stable view after relevant writers have stopped or from an appropriate snapshot, so the patch and reported version describe the same state. Resolve and validate eligible paths and artifact types within that view; a generated link must not turn an approved export into a read of an unrelated host file.

Do not archive the raw upper tree as though it were the deliverable. Deletion markers, renames, metadata, generated files, caches, and possible sensitive contents need interpretation and filtering. An exported patch is a proposed deliverable, not proof of acceptance; check records must retain which source and checks they describe. Any later application to a shared repository still needs its own authorization and action-time preconditions.

The remaining private state can then be discarded under the reset policy developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling. Detaching a filesystem view does not by itself reclaim its resources or establish that it is ready for another tenant. Crash-survival requirements for the workspace and its trajectory record belong to @sec-vol3-durable-execution.

Controlled artifact export governs one path out of the workspace. It does not govern every outbound channel available to code running inside it. Source files and test artifacts may remain sensitive even when brokered credentials never enter the workspace. The next section therefore constrains network access independently of storage continuity.

## Egress Control {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-network}

Return to the injected README with credential brokering in place. The command cannot read the broker's credential from the guest, but it can still read source files needed for the repair. Sending those files to an unintended recipient would disclose information without escaping the workspace or stealing a key. **Egress control** governs the channels through which executing code communicates outside its envelope. It must constrain the actual communication path, not depend on the code choosing to use a preferred client.

### Enforce the path outside the guest

A task that needs no external communication can run without an outbound network path. A task that must fetch dependencies or source needs a narrower arrangement. The runtime can expose a task-scoped service adapter, or permit access through a controlled network gateway. In either case, code inside the sandbox must not be able to reach the same external resources through an unchecked alternative.

For a networked guest, this means enforcing its permitted routes and protocols outside the guest's control. Direct sockets, additional interfaces, alternate address families, name-resolution services, and host services reachable through local channels all belong in the reachability review. A local host adapter that forwards arbitrary requests can bypass an otherwise effective network filter. The boundary must cover such forwarding as well as ordinary packets.

Setting `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY` configures clients that honor those settings. It does not prevent a program from ignoring them and opening a direct connection. Likewise, a packet filter sees destination addresses; it cannot tell whether the program obtained an address from a hostname or typed the address literally. Network enforcement constrains reachable endpoints, while a higher-level mediator interprets the requested service and operation. Testing the design therefore includes attempted bypasses, not merely a successful request through the preferred proxy. @Fig-vol3-network-egress applies the two enforcement points to four requests from the guest.

::: {#fig-vol3-network-egress fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest**: The packet filter sees only addresses and ports, so it admits connections to the mediator and drops a direct socket or a lookup sent toward an outside resolver, whatever name the program had in mind. The mediator interprets the request. It resolves its own fixed destinations, admits the repository fetch, and adds the brokered credential, while a push or a request for another repository fails the operation grant at the same hostname. A mediator can inspect or change methods, paths, and bodies only if it makes the upstream request itself or terminates TLS; a proxy that merely forwards encrypted traffic cannot." fig-alt="Four columns labeled guest with no default route, packet filter that sees addresses and ports, mediator that binds name, operation, and fields, and outside the guest. Four requests leave the guest. A fetch of the approved repository passes the filter to the adapter, is admitted by the mediator, and reaches the approved repository with a credential added by the mediator. A push or request for another repository passes the filter but is marked operation denied at the mediator. A direct socket to a literal address is marked dropped at the filter, and a metadata or other host is marked not reached. An arbitrary name lookup from the guest is marked no resolver route at the filter, and an external DNS server is marked not reached."}
![](images/svg/network_egress_defense_in_depth.svg)
:::

### Separate destination, operation, and data

Permission to contact a service answers only one part of the disclosure question. A source-hosting service may offer repository reads, pushes, issue comments, and public uploads under the same hostname. The task's permission to fetch its repository does not authorize those other operations. Even a permitted operation can carry information the task should not send. @Tbl-vol3-egress-filtering separates these decisions.

| Policy scope           | Question                                                              | What the restriction does not establish                     |
|:-----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
